A bibliometric analysis was employed to characterize MCs. Both an analysis of published case studies and a survey on MCs for SD were conducted to identify the provision of MCs for SD. The findings identified that while some institutions have been offering MCs for several years, many do not or have only recently started offering them. Advancing MCs for SD will require stronger institutional coordination, collaboration with external stakeholders, clearer policy alignment, and sustained attention to educational quality and equity. Successfully implemented cases and critical challenges surrounding the implementation of MCs were discussed, and recommendations were provided with strategic measures to address some of the key barriers hindering successful implementation of MCs for SD.

title: Comparative analysis of students’ learning satisfaction and gains: special blended synchronous versus traditional classrooms in rural schools
abstract: Abstract Information technology has been increasingly leveraged to promote educational equity in less-developed regions. In China, the blended synchronous classroom (BSC) enables high-quality teachers to simultaneously instruct students in their own classrooms and those in remote weak schools, thereby addressing the shortage of specialized teachers in rural areas. This study examines an optimized variant—the special blended synchronous classroom (SBSC) environment—in which a single specialized teacher delivers Music and Art instruction to students in two or three rural primary schools simultaneously, with each remote classroom supported by an auxiliary teacher. Employing a quasi-experimental design, this study investigates the factors influencing students’ learning satisfaction in both the SBSC and traditional face-to-face (TFTF) environments, and compares students’ learning gains in Music and Art courses between the two settings. Data were collected from 824 Grade 2 and Grade 3 students via questionnaires and analyzed using SPSS 22.0 and SmartPLS 3.0. The results reveal that, in both environments, learning motivation and learning strategies significantly predicted learning satisfaction, whereas learning attitude did not. Regarding learning gains, SBSC students achieved significantly higher learning gains in singing, music theory, painting, sketching and composition, and handicraft compared with their TFTF peers, whereas no significant difference was found in musical instrument performance. This study contributes to the design of technology-enhanced classroom environments that expand access to high-quality Music and Art education in rural primary schools, offering empirical evidence for educational equity initiatives.

title: Student epistemic agency in AI-mediated practices
abstract: Abstract Little is known about students’ epistemic agency in relation to AI-mediated practices. This study was conducted in a Swedish school that had started the pilot project “AI on the schedule” for compulsory school students, for whom the national curricula do not include AI training. A survey covering the aspects of source evaluation, data privacy, algorithmic manipulation, transparency, responsibility, and governance was distributed to these year 7 students ( n = 47). The data was analysed through cross-tabulations of question pairs. This revealed how epistemic agency varied across aspects within individual students. Results show that students demonstrated strong epistemic agency in certain areas but weak agency in others, for example, in data privacy and algorithmic manipulation, even when these had been part of earlier instruction. The contribution of the study is that epistemic agency in AI-mediated practices is not a unified construct: the data suggest distinct output-directed and system-directed dimensions, each with its own area of application. This has implications for instruction and guidance when integrating AI into K-12 teaching.

title: Exploring student and teacher perspectives on critical thinking with generative AI: early insights from the EduPartnerAI platform
abstract: Abstract The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education has raised important questions about its implications for students’ analytical reasoning and independent judgment. ChatGPT, a generative AI model capable of producing human-like responses, is widely used in academic contexts, yet its educational value requires careful evaluation. This paper presents and evaluates EduPartnerAI, a platform that integrates ChatGPT into student assignments and is designed to encourage critical engagement with AI-generated content. The platform records student-AI interactions, requires students to reflect on ChatGPT’s outputs, and provides teachers with tools to review observable indicators of student reasoning and AI response quality. An exploratory study involving 61 undergraduate students was conducted, relying on student reflection questionnaires, a usability survey, teacher evaluations, and an analysis of recorded interactions. Students generally perceived ChatGPT as a useful learning tool that provided clear explanations and practical examples, although some recognized that its responses could be overly general or incomplete. The teacher observed that students asked relevant questions and effectively incorporated AI-generated content into their assignments but experienced some difficulties with error detection, independent judgment, and critical evaluation. The teacher also judged ChatGPT’s outputs to be largely relevant, clear, and accurate, with few instances of bias or misleading information. Overall, the findings provide preliminary insights into student and teacher perspectives and observable patterns of engagement, highlighting both the educational potential of generative AI and the need for appropriate instructional scaffolding.
